outcomeNoiseSigma.note: Lognormal sigma of per-round combat effectiveness noise for one side. That residual still contains unmodelled quality, terrain and posture (which the engine models explicitly), so pure chance is a part of it: mid 0.25 assumes about half the residual variance is chance (0.34 x sqrt(0.5) = 0.24). Low keeps the current engine value. The fit is per battle, not per round: a battle of n independent rounds averages noise down by sqrt(n), so a per-round sigma could be up to sqrt(n) higher; calibrate against the backtest spread before going above 0.34.

armyCollapseMorale.note: UNSOURCED MODEL-DEFINITION CONSTANT: mid 0.15 is the engine's original definition (ENGINE.md 12), restored after QA round 2 found that 0.2 decided gate cases (Six-Day, Gulf War). Backtests are reported across 0.10-0.25 (scripts/backtest.ts --sweep). Earlier reasoning for 0.2: Engine-internal 0..1 side morale below which the army ceases resisting. No source measures this scale. Educated guess: morale in the engine falls with the share of starting strength lost, and the cases above collapse at 30-60% losses, which suggests a threshold somewhat above 0.15; Dupuy's finding that defeat is mostly caused by maneuver, not casualties (https://dupuyinstitute.org/2017/06/23/battle-outcomes-casualty-rates-as-a-measure-of-defeat/), argues for the morale trigger firing before the personnel trigger. WHAT WOULD SET IT: an observable that maps to the engine morale scale, e.g. the daily rate of surrender, desertion or refusal of orders, read (1) at known battle breakpoints, where morale.breakpoint and defeatShock already define the scale, and (2) in the days before whole-army collapses outside the backtest set (Russia 1917, Austria-Hungary 1918, Italy at Caporetto 1917, Yugoslavia 1941, East Pakistan 1971); the threshold is then the engine morale whose observable matches the collapse cases. No fetched source gives such a series; left grade D.

attrition.note: Combat-power ratio (attacker:defender) an attrition-doctrine AI (maneuver weight 0) masses at the attack point before it attacks. All figures below are LOCAL (attack point, sector or avenue of approach), not theatre. Mid 3: FM 5-0 The Operations Process (2010) table B-1 'Historical minimum planning ratios', attack against a prepared or fortified position 3:1, applied per task and avenue of approach two levels down, in relative combat power including intangibles (paras B-89, B-90); Mearsheimer, 'Assessing the Conventional Balance: The 3:1 Rule and Its Critics', International Security 13:4 (1989) p.54 (https://www.mearsheimer.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/A0013.pdf): a local advantage of at least 3:1 in combat power to break through at a specific point, for breakthrough battles only; FM 100-2-1 The Soviet Army: Operations and Tactics (1984) p.2-11 (https://irp.fas.org/doddir/army/fm100-2-1.pdf): contemporary Soviet writings put the aggregate combat-power ratio for an attack at about 3:1, counting all forces and fires the commander can bring to bear on the sector. Low 2.5: FM 5-0 hasty attack 2.5:1 (FM 100-2-1 adds that the ratio actually at the FEBA may be as small as 2:1). High 5: FM 100-2-1, post-1945 Soviet main-attack weighting of 3-5:1 in tanks and 4-5:1 in personnel (6-8:1 in artillery) on the main-attack sector. Critics: Epstein (International Security 12:4, 1988) disputes the rule with historical cases (as summarised by Mearsheimer 1989); the Dupuy Institute division-level database (752 cases 1904-1991, local engagements, raw strength; https://dupuyinstitute.org/2019/10/31/tests-using-the-752-case-division-level-data-base/) has attackers winning 55% at 1.0-1.49:1 and 83% at 2.5-2.99:1, so 3:1 is a conservative planning norm rather than an outcome threshold, which is what an attrition doctrine plans to. Not used: theatre-level figures (Dupuy Institute Campaign Data Base, 196 campaigns 1905-1991, attacker wins at an average 2.28:1, https://dupuyinstitute.org/2024/04/23/analysis-for-force-ratios-using-the-campaign-data-base-cadb/) and the lead-element penetration ratio 18:1 of the proposed ATP 5-0.2 (2019), which is only reported second-hand.

maneuver.note: Combat-power ratio (attacker:defender) a maneuver-doctrine AI (maneuver weight 1) masses at the attack point before it attacks; LOCAL, not theatre. No doctrine publishes a maneuver-specific ratio, so derived: mid 1.5 = the local 3:1 norm (attrition leaf) divided by a surprise multiplier of 2.0, the middle of Dupuy's 1.5-2.5 (HERO, Handbook on Ground Forces Attrition in Modern Warfare, 1986, https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/citations/ADA278728: an attacker expecting surprise 'would be willing to attack with less than a three-to-one superiority'); the range 3/2.5 to 3/1.5 is 1.2-2.0. Low 1.0: FM 5-0 (2010) table B-1, counterattack into a flank 1:1 (local). High 2.5: FM 5-0 hasty attack 2.5:1 (local). Cross-check against outcomes, not planning norms: Dupuy Institute division-level database (752 cases 1904-1991, local engagements, raw strength; https://dupuyinstitute.org/2019/10/31/tests-using-the-752-case-division-level-data-base/) attackers won 59% at 1.5-1.99:1 and 55% at 1.0-1.49:1; ETO 1944-45 division engagements (116 cases, Lawrence, War by Numbers p.10; https://dupuyinstitute.org/2020/12/24/force-ratios-and-crts/) attacks at 1.15-1.88:1 succeeded 79%. Dupuy (HERO 1986) also credits German WWII and Israeli attacks below 3:1 to troop quality; the AI already measures power with quality, training and command, so only the surprise and flank effect is used here, to avoid counting quality twice. Grade C: a derivation from cited figures, not a stated doctrine norm.

formationLoss.note: Fraction of a targeted formation lost per strike. One ~20 kt weapon -> 18-24 km2 / 420-520 km2 = 3.5-6%; 100-300 kt (area scales W^2/3, x2.9-6) -> 10-35%; first use targets the densest concentration, so mid 0.15.

techLevels.label: Neolithic / Chalcolithic
techLevels.description: Stone weapons, simple bow; no armor; rafts and canoes; palisades; porters; runners.

techLevels.label: Early Bronze Age
techLevels.description: Copper/bronze maces and spears; leather armor, copper helmets; oared riverboats; mudbrick walls; donkeys and carts; runners and signal fires.

techLevels.label: Late Bronze Age
techLevels.description: Composite bow, war chariot, bronze swords; bronze scale armor; oared war galleys; stone citadels; ox wagons and depots; couriers.

techLevels.label: Classical Iron Age
techLevels.description: Iron weapons, torsion artillery, sarissa; bronze/iron cuirass, mail; triremes and quinqueremes; ashlar city walls, siege towers; engineered roads, depot system; mounted relay posts.

techLevels.label: High Middle Ages
techLevels.description: Crossbow, longbow, couched lance, trebuchet; plate-and-mail, barding; cogs and galleys; concentric castles; river transport, granaries; relay horses (yam).

techLevels.label: Early gunpowder (pike and shot)
techLevels.description: Arquebus/musket, pike, field cannon; half-armor, cuirass; galleons, early ships of the line; trace italienne; magazines, canal transport; couriers, early postal systems.

techLevels.label: Napoleonic
techLevels.description: Flintlock musket, 12-pdr gun, Gribeauval system; no armor or cuirass only; 74-gun ships of the line; Vauban-type forts; magazines plus requisition; semaphore telegraph.

techLevels.label: Industrial (pre-WWI)
techLevels.description: Magazine rifle, machine gun, QF artillery; armored cars, steel helmet (1915); dreadnoughts, steam; concrete forts, trenches; railways; electric telegraph, telephone. ISR 7 = aerial reconnaissance (1914), air 7 = 1914 aircraft.

techLevels.label: Second World War
techLevels.description: Tanks, dive bombers, radar-directed AA; rolled homogeneous armor; carriers, radar, submarines; concrete lines; motor transport and rail; radio at company level. ISR 8 = radar.

techLevels.label: Late Cold War
techLevels.description: Guided missiles, MBTs with fire control, jets; composite armor; nuclear submarines, Aegis; hardened shelters; containerised logistics, airlift; satellite comms and data links. ISR 9 = satellites, cyber 9 = 1990 networks.

techLevels.label: 2026 frontier
techLevels.description: Precision munitions, drones, hypersonics; active protection; networked fleets, USVs; layered air defence; just-in-time, global sealift; networked C4ISR. ISR 10 = persistent drone/space ISR, air 10 = 5th generation, cyber 10 = state cyber forces.
